strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in language-based 3D perception and demonstrates a substantial accuracy–latency improvement. On ASE, the 10-head SSD model reduces decoding latency from 382 to 75 ms while retaining nearly the same mean F1 (0.912 versus 0.915). On Structured3D, latency decreases from 1176 to 211 ms while mean F1 improves from 0.774 to 0.790.

The proposed combination is technically sensible: multi-token prediction reduces autoregressive iterations, numerical-tolerance verification accommodates geometric outputs, and shared projections and heads limit parameter growth. The SSD model uses 15.05M decoder parameters versus 14.00M for SceneScript and 26.43M for unshared 10-head MTP.

Table 3 provides useful component-level evidence. Numerical tolerance reduces SSD latency from 90 to 80 ms with essentially unchanged F1. Head sharing substantially reduces parameters without degrading accuracy. CGD improves on the evaluated softmax-based filtering alternatives, achieving 91 ms and 0.911 F1 versus 112–116 ms and 0.908–0.909 F1.

Evaluation includes two datasets, validation and test results on ASE, a retrained SceneScript baseline stronger than the released model, and qualitative comparisons. Although the methodological advances are incremental, the measured decoding gains and parameter savings constitute a useful computer-vision contribution and support weak acceptance.
weaknesses: The accounting of decoder iterations needs clarification. Section 3.2 and Figure 4 describe SSD as a drafting pass followed by a verification pass, yet the tables report approximately nine accepted tokens per decoder inference with ten heads. This appears to count a draft–verify cycle or rely on unstated reuse between verification and subsequent drafting. Pseudocode and an explicit definition of the denominator are needed to substantiate the tokens-per-inference claim; this ambiguity does not itself invalidate the reported wall-clock measurements.

Several consequential reproduction details are missing from the supplied manuscript: the CGD acceptance threshold epsilon, the inference sampling rule, the physical or quantization scale corresponding to tau = 2, and whether confidence-training targets use teacher-forced or drafted preceding tokens. Timing specifies hardware but omits inference batch size, precision, caching, and synchronization details. These omissions affect the central accuracy–speed tradeoff.

The incremental value of CGD over SSD is limited by the reported results. CGD is slower and larger at both head counts on both datasets, with mostly similar accuracy; its clearest accuracy advantage is the eight-head Structured3D result. Eliminating a separate verification pass is conceptually attractive, but the paper does not demonstrate an application-level benefit from this property. Threshold sweeps would also make comparisons against ProductThre and SoftmaxThre more convincing than single operating points.

The evidence supports acceleration of SceneScript layout decoding, rather than the broader claims about perception generalists. Both datasets are synthetic indoor datasets, and no additional perception task or backbone is evaluated. Furthermore, parameter counts and latency cover the decoder rather than the complete point-cloud-to-layout pipeline, so the reported fivefold gains should not be interpreted as end-to-end system speedups.

Accuracy-preservation claims require some qualification. ASE mean F1 decreases from 0.915 to 0.912 with SSD and to 0.910 with CGD at ten heads, without repeated-run uncertainty estimates. Averaging F1 over distance thresholds up to one meter also leaves unclear whether relaxed numerical acceptance affects strict geometric precision. These are limitations on the strength of the accuracy claims, rather than evidence that the substantial efficiency gains lack value.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful bottleneck in language-based 3D reconstruction and demonstrates a substantial practical improvement. On ASE, SSD with n=10 reduces decoding latency from 382 ms to 75 ms while retaining nearly the same mean F1 (0.915 versus 0.912). On Structured3D, latency falls from 1176 ms to 211 ms while F1 improves from 0.774 to 0.790. These results support acceptance for a focused efficiency contribution.

The proposed adaptations are appropriate for structured geometric outputs: numerical tolerance avoids rejecting geometrically similar predictions, learned confidence estimates approximate verification, and shared prediction heads limit parameter growth. The SSD decoder requires 15.05M parameters compared with 14.00M for SceneScript and 26.43M for unshared 10-head MTP.

Table 3 provides meaningful component evidence. Increasing numerical tolerance from zero to two reduces latency from 90 ms to 80 ms with essentially unchanged F1. Head sharing substantially reduces parameters without degrading accuracy. CGD also improves latency over the tested product-probability and softmax-threshold alternatives at comparable accuracy.

The evaluation includes two datasets, both released and retrained SceneScript baselines, multiple prediction horizons, class-specific metrics, and qualitative comparisons. The stronger retrained baseline makes the central comparison more persuasive than comparison against the released checkpoint alone.
weaknesses: The headline token-throughput metric is insufficiently explained. Section 3.2 and Figure 4 describe separate drafting and verification decoder calls, whereas Tables 1–2 report approximately nine accepted tokens per decoder inference with n=10. If both calls are counted separately, this does not follow from the described algorithm. A schedule explaining any reuse or fusion is necessary to reconcile the metric. This ambiguity weakens the throughput claim, although it does not by itself invalidate the separately reported wall-clock speedups.

Important reproduction details are missing from the supplied manuscript: the CGD acceptance threshold epsilon, the numerical-token quantization needed to interpret tau=2, and whether confidence targets compare predictions under teacher-forced or drafted prefixes. The latter matters because agreement under ground-truth context need not predict agreement during inference. Timing also lacks inference batch size, precision, cache configuration, and measurement protocol. Reported latency and parameter counts explicitly cover the decoder, so the results do not establish equivalent end-to-end system savings.

The methodological advance is incremental over established multi-token prediction, blockwise/speculative decoding, and parameter sharing. Much of the headline accuracy recovery compares against MTP without filtering. Although Table 3 includes an exact-verification variant, it does not provide a fully matched unshared MTP plus standard exact-verification baseline, making the combined benefit beyond conventional speculative decoding less cleanly isolated.

The practical advantage of CGD over the paper's SSD variant remains limited. At n=10, CGD is slower and larger on both datasets, with lower ASE F1 and equal Structured3D F1. At n=8 it offers a small Structured3D accuracy improvement, but its claimed on-the-fly benefit is not evaluated through a streaming or responsiveness metric. Figures 7–8 illustrate acceptance behavior rather than directly establishing confidence calibration or correctness.

The evidence supports SceneScript-based layout estimation, rather than the broader perception-generalist claims. Both datasets concern indoor layouts, and no other task or backbone is tested. Additionally, F1 is averaged over distance thresholds up to one meter; threshold-specific results would better establish whether relaxed numerical verification preserves fine geometric accuracy. These limitations constrain the scope of the contribution but do not outweigh the demonstrated decoding improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in language-based 3D perception with a convincing accuracy–latency tradeoff. On ASE, the 10-head SSD model reduces decoding latency from 382 to 75 ms while changing mean F1 from 0.915 to 0.912; on Structured3D, latency falls from 1176 to 211 ms while F1 improves from 0.774 to 0.790.
The structured-output adaptations are useful: numerical-tolerance verification, learned confidence-based acceptance, and shared prediction heads form a coherent approach to accelerating SceneScript.

Table 3 provides meaningful component ablations. Numerical tolerance reduces SSD latency from 90 to 80 ms with essentially unchanged accuracy, while parameter sharing reduces the SSD decoder from 23.67M to 15.05M parameters without degrading accuracy.

CGD improves over the evaluated scoring-based alternatives: it achieves 91 ms and 0.911 F1 versus 112–116 ms and 0.908–0.909 F1 for probability-threshold methods. Comparisons include both released and retrained SceneScript models, and qualitative results support the quantitative findings.

Overall, the substantial measured decoding gains across two datasets support weak acceptance. The contribution has practical value despite being an incremental adaptation of established decoding techniques.
weaknesses: The accounting behind the headline tokens-per-inference claim is unclear. Section 3.2 describes separate drafting and verification passes for SSD, yet Table 1 reports 8.99 accepted tokens per decoder inference with 10 heads. The manuscript needs to explain whether verification is excluded or combined with subsequent drafting. This affects interpretation of throughput, although the reported wall-clock improvements remain substantial.

Important reproducibility details are missing: the CGD threshold epsilon, the inference sampling rule, and whether confidence-training targets use ground-truth prefixes or drafted prefixes. The latter matters because first-head agreement under teacher forcing need not predict agreement during inference. Timing details such as batching, precision, and caching are also unspecified.

The strongest results use SSD, whereas CGD is consistently slower and adds more parameters. For example, the 10-head ASE models take 75 versus 89 ms and use 15.05M versus 16.10M parameters. The practical advantage of CGD's on-the-fly verification beyond its implementation structure is therefore not demonstrated.

The evidence supports decoder acceleration for layout estimation, rather than general perception acceleration. Both datasets are synthetic indoor datasets, only one task and backbone are evaluated, and reported latency and parameter counts exclude the encoder. Claims about preserving generalist versatility and overall system efficiency exceed the demonstrated scope.

Accuracy is averaged across matching tolerances up to one meter. Since the method explicitly permits numerical discrepancies, results at strict tolerances would better establish preservation of geometric precision. No variability estimates are provided, so small F1 differences should not be interpreted as decisive improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in language-based 3D perception and demonstrates a useful accuracy–latency trade-off. On ASE layout estimation, SSD reduces decoding latency from 382 ms to 75 ms while retaining nearly identical test F1 (0.915 versus 0.912; Table 1). This substantial efficiency improvement supports acceptance despite the incremental nature of several components.

The benefits extend across datasets and tasks. On Structured3D, SSD improves F1 from 0.774 to 0.790 while reducing decoding time from 1176 ms to 211 ms. On real-world SceneCAD, it preserves layout F1 at 0.556 and improves detection F1@0.50 from 0.461 to 0.544, with substantially lower latency.

The parameter-sharing mechanism is effective and supported by ablations. Table 4 shows that sharing reduces SSD decoder parameters from 23.67M to 15.05M without reducing accuracy. The resulting SSD model adds only 7.5% decoder parameters over SceneScript.

The experiments meaningfully examine numerical tolerance, head sharing, confidence thresholds, supervision targets, and prediction horizon. CGD improves over both softmax-based filtering baselines, and the supplement reports saturation with additional heads and qualitative failure cases. Architecture and training descriptions provide a useful basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: The methodological advance over existing MTP and speculative decoding is relatively modest. In Table 4, exact-match SSD already achieves 90 ms latency and 0.911 F1; numerical tolerance improves this to 80 ms and 0.912. CGD achieves 91 ms and 0.911 with more parameters, and is generally slower than SSD in the main tables. Its advantage over softmax filtering is supported, but its practical advantage over SSD is limited.

The efficiency evidence concerns decoder latency and decoder parameters, excluding the point-cloud encoder and other pipeline costs. End-to-end acceleration therefore remains unknown. Timing details such as inference batch size, caching, synchronization, and repetitions are insufficiently specified. Additionally, SSD is described as requiring drafting and verification passes, but the reported approximately nine accepted tokens per decoder inference does not explain how verification passes are counted.

ASE object detection is evaluated against TR3D-generated annotations rather than independent ground truth (Section 4.1). These results establish agreement with a detector-derived target, which limits conclusions about actual detection accuracy. SceneCAD provides valuable real-data evidence, but the pseudo-label generation settings and label quality are not sufficiently characterized.

Claims of preserving accuracy need qualification under matched training budgets. MTP receives additional training after NTP initialization. Table S5 reports ASE test F1 of 0.920 for SceneScript trained for 90 epochs, compared with 0.912 for the headline 10-head SSD configuration. The speed–accuracy trade-off remains attractive, but the additional baseline result should inform the main comparison.

CGD learns agreement with first-head predictions under teacher forcing, whereas inference uses generated prefixes. The paper does not directly measure confidence calibration or erroneous acceptance under this distribution shift. The softmax histograms show different acceptance behavior, but do not by themselves establish better reliability estimation. Numerical-tolerance decoding also lacks exact-output preservation, so its reliability is empirical rather than guaranteed.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck in language-based 3D perception and demonstrates a substantial improvement in the accuracy–latency trade-off. On ASE layout estimation, SSD reduces decoding latency from 382 to 75 ms while retaining nearly the same test F1 (0.915 versus 0.912; Table 1). This is a useful contribution even without improving absolute accuracy.

The benefits extend across three datasets and two tasks. On Structured3D, SSD improves F1 from 0.774 to 0.790 while reducing decoding latency from 1176 to 211 ms (Table 2). On real-world SceneCAD, it preserves layout F1 at 0.556 with a 2.57× decoding speedup and improves object detection results (Table 3).

The component studies provide meaningful support for the design. Table 4 isolates numerical tolerance, parameter sharing, and confidence-based filtering. Shared heads reduce decoder parameters from 23.67M to 15.05M for SSD without degrading accuracy; CGD improves the measured accuracy–latency trade-off over the tested softmax and cumulative-probability filtering baselines.

The supplement adds useful threshold sweeps, larger-head experiments, confidence-supervision comparisons, training settings, and failure cases. Overall, the supported practical gains favor weak acceptance, despite reservations about novelty and efficiency accounting.
weaknesses: The token-throughput accounting needs clarification. Section 3.2 and Figure 4 describe separate drafting and verification decoder passes for SSD, yet Table 1 reports approximately nine accepted tokens per 'decoder inference' with ten heads. Without an explanation of whether verification is counted or combined with subsequent drafting, this statistic does not clearly support the headline claim of nine tokens per decoder step. The reported wall-clock improvements remain valuable, but this ambiguity affects a central explanatory claim.

The efficiency results cover decoding rather than the complete perception pipeline. Section 4.1 explicitly excludes encoder time from latency and encoder parameters from model size. Consequently, the approximately 5× gains should not be interpreted as end-to-end speedups. Timing details such as inference batch size, cache handling, synchronization, and variability are also insufficiently specified for a paper centered on inference efficiency.

The originality is primarily an adaptation and integration of established MTP and speculative-decoding ideas. CGD is the more distinctive component, but its practical advantage over SSD is limited: on ASE layout estimation with eight heads, CGD takes 92 ms and 16.10M parameters versus SSD's 81 ms and 15.05M, with identical test F1 (Table 1). Its on-the-fly verification is interesting, but does not generally produce the best measured trade-off. The approximately 7.5% parameter-overhead claim applies to SSD; CGD adds approximately 15%.

ASE object detection is evaluated against TR3D-generated pseudo-annotations rather than independent ground truth (Section 4.1). These results demonstrate agreement with the labeling detector and preservation under acceleration, but provide weaker evidence of actual detection accuracy. SceneCAD supplies useful independent support, although the broader detection claims should reflect this limitation.

Claims of unchanged or improved accuracy require qualification. Table S5 shows that extending the ASE SceneScript baseline from 60 to 90 epochs raises test F1 from 0.915 to 0.920, compared with 0.912 for the headline ten-head SSD configuration. MTP receives additional training after NTP initialization, and an analogous training-budget control is not reported for object detection. Without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, small differences and the proposed regularization explanation are not firmly established.

strengths: The paper makes a useful, empirically supported contribution to efficient structured 3D prediction. On ASE layout estimation, SSD reduces decoding latency from 382 ms to 75 ms while retaining nearly identical test F1 (0.915 versus 0.912). This substantial efficiency gain provides a stronger case for acceptance than the limitations provide for rejection.

Results extend across synthetic and real-world datasets and two tasks. On Structured3D, SSD improves layout F1 from 0.774 to 0.790 while reducing latency from 1176 ms to 211 ms. On SceneCAD, it preserves layout F1 at 0.556 and improves detection F1@0.50 from 0.461 to 0.544.

The ablations substantiate the proposed components. Table 4 shows that numerical tolerance improves SSD latency, shared heads substantially reduce parameters without degrading accuracy, and learned confidence filtering outperforms the tested probability-threshold alternatives in the accuracy–latency trade-off.

The presentation and supplementary material provide useful architectural diagrams, training settings, threshold sweeps, confidence-supervision comparisons, and failure cases. The disclosure of pseudo-label generation and the longer-training baseline helps readers assess the evidence.
weaknesses: The originality is primarily an effective adaptation and integration of existing multi-token prediction and speculative decoding. The distinctive CGD component has a limited demonstrated advantage over SSD: on ASE with eight heads it is slower (92 versus 81 ms), uses more parameters (16.10M versus 15.05M), and achieves the same test F1. Its practical benefit from verification within the same pass is less clearly established than the overall acceleration.

Efficiency measurements cover decoder latency and decoder parameters, rather than the complete point-cloud processing pipeline. Consequently, the reported fivefold gains do not establish equivalent end-to-end acceleration. Timing details such as batch size, cache handling, and synchronization are insufficiently specified. Additionally, the definition of accepted tokens per decoder inference needs reconciliation with SSD's described separate drafting and verification passes.

ASE object detection is evaluated against TR3D-generated annotations, so its high F1 primarily establishes agreement with a pseudo-labeling teacher rather than independently annotated detection quality. SceneCAD supplies valuable real-world evidence, but the detection conclusions remain narrower than the layout evidence.

The claims of preserving accuracy and adding only approximately 7.5% parameters need qualification by configuration. The latter applies to SSD, whereas CGD adds approximately 15%. Table S5 also gives a longer-trained SceneScript test F1 of 0.920, compared with 0.912 for the fastest highlighted ASE configuration. This remains an attractive trade-off, but it is not strictly accuracy-neutral, and repeated-run uncertainty is not reported.

The confidence analysis does not directly establish calibration or prediction correctness: accepting low-softmax tokens and rejecting high-softmax tokens only demonstrates different selection behavior. CGD learns agreement under teacher-forced contexts, while inference uses generated contexts; the effect of this mismatch is not measured. The task-level ablations support usefulness, but the stronger interpretation of confidence as robust uncertainty estimation is less well supported.
